problem: Zero-shot object navigation methods depend on ground-truth depth and pose (and global maps), which limits real-world use, and they cannot exploit a short offline traversal video of the environment as visual in-context prior.
motivation: Real robots have noisy or missing depth and pose, and cheap RGB videos of a new environment are easy to obtain. Recent 3D foundation models (MASt3R, VGGT) make RGB-only metric reconstruction feasible, so a navigation system could run on monocular RGB and use a walkthrough video as an environmental preview to cut exploration.
key_idea: Build a keyframe-based memory bank with MASt3R-SLAM and fuse CLIP/GroundingDINO semantics into a point cloud and value map, so a VLM-value-driven frontier/object planner runs on monocular RGB only and can ingest an offline video simply by pre-filling the memory.
insight: Feeding an offline traversal video into the same memory bank, with no retraining, raises SR from 44.0 to 58.0 and SPL from 16.4 to 30.2 while cutting average steps from 171.4 to 110.2, so visual in-context adaptation works through memory alone. The hierarchical high-level planner helps (SR 42.7 to 39.8 when removed), and MASt3R-SLAM is qualitatively more robust than VGGT and VGGT-SLAM for long sequences. The detector choice matters little (DINO 42.7 vs YOLO-World 42.3).
method: Online RGB reconstruction: MASt3R-SLAM provides keyframe pointmaps, ray-based tracking, and loop closure over a pose graph, giving dense geometry and pose from RGB only
Real-scale recovery: fit a ground plane by RANSAC on the lowest 20% of points, estimate camera height, and scale the map by h_real/h_est

Semantic point cloud: GroundingDINO boxes + MobileSAM masks filtered by SLAM confidence, CLIP features per object, association by weighted CLIP + point-cloud IoU similarity, and fusion by weighted feature average and max confidence
2D maps: project the 3D cloud to an obstacle map and an exploration map to get frontiers, plus a value map V=max(s_obj, s_img) from CLIP similarity of objects and keyframes to the target

High-level adaptive planner: hierarchical priority (confident object as final target, low-confidence object as temporary waypoint, otherwise the highest-value frontier), with reachability checks and a dynamic blacklist for unreachable spots and false positives
Low-level planner: Fast Marching Method local path planning toward the subgoal in closed loop
Contextual video adaptation: the offline video is processed into the same keyframe memory bank before navigation, without architectural changes

setting.backbone: MASt3R-SLAM + GroundingDINO + MobileSAM + CLIP (all frozen, pretrained)
setting.observation: monocular RGB (640x480, camera at 0.88 m in Habitat)
setting.action_space: low-level discrete: move_forward 25 cm, turn 30°, look_up, look_down, stop, driven by FMM toward waypoints
setting.privileged: none (camera height is used as a scale prior; in the contextual setting an offline walkthrough video of the same scene is provided)

numbers.eval_set_note: 10 single-floor HM3Dv2 scenes, 279 episodes, 6 goal categories, 300-step limit
numbers.extra: RGB only; no depth or pose; 300 max steps
numbers.evidence: Table I: RANGER (300) RGB, 42.7 SR, 17.8 SPL, 172.80 Avg Steps

numbers.eval_set_note: same 10 scenes, 100 episodes started near the end of the offline video, 6 categories
numbers.extra: uses a teleoperated offline traversal video of the same scene as context

numbers_note: Only a self-selected subset of HM3D (10 scenes) was evaluated, and the only baseline is L3MVN with depth and pose. No official HM3D val split numbers are reported.
results: With RGB only and a 300-step limit, RANGER reaches 42.7 SR and 17.8 SPL on a 279-episode HM3D subset, beating L3MVN (300) at 39.4 SR and L3MVN (500) at 42.3 SR, both of which use depth and pose. An offline video lifts SR to 58.0 from 44.0 and SPL to 30.2 from 16.4. The system also runs at about 1 Hz on a Unitree G1 humanoid in real rooms, shown qualitatively.
limitations: Keyframe memory grows without bound, increasing storage and compute, and needs better memory management
Reconstruction and localization are not robust enough for complex or dynamic environments
Evaluation is small and non-standard (10 scenes, one baseline, no quantitative real-world results)
